c.tagline: Prairie crossroads at the forks of two rivers - human-rights museum, French quarter, and legendary cold winters.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares start around C$3.90 plus per-km charges; Uber and Lyft operate citywide and are often cheaper. Cabs can be scarce in bad weather, so booking ahead helps.

emergency.note: 911 is the single emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance across Canada; Health Links (204-788-8200) is Manitoba's 24/7 non-emergency health advice line.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Caution in parts of the North End and downtown at night — higher crime than most Canadian cities

hood_desc: Winnipeg's business and events core around Portage and Main, home to the RBC Convention Centre, Canada Life Centre arena, and the enclosed downtown Skywalk; the central, transit-friendly base for first-time visitors.

A National Historic Site of beautifully preserved early-1900s warehouses now filled with galleries, boutiques, coffee shops, theatres, and buzzing restaurants; best for architecture, arts, and dining.
A compact, trendy neighbourhood just south of downtown packed with indie bars, patios, live music, and eclectic shops; Winnipeg's go-to district for nightlife and going out.
The historic French Quarter across the Red River, centred on the St. Boniface Cathedral ruins, the Riel House, and riverside Provencher Boulevard bistros; a calm, culture-rich residential base.
A west-end shopping and sports hub around CF Polo Park mall and Assiniboine Park, with big-box retail, the football stadium, and easy airport access; convenient for shoppers and families.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 6am-1am, with reduced frequency evenings and weekends; the BLUE rapid-transit line is the fastest link between downtown and the southwest.
transit.note: Winnipeg has no subway, tram, or commuter rail - Winnipeg Transit buses plus the BLUE Line rapid-transit (Southwest Transitway) are the network. It's a car-oriented, spread-out city, so many visitors rent a car or use ride-hail apps.
transit.pay: Tap a Peggo smart card, pay cash on board (exact change; about C$3.35 an adult fare), or use contactless payment on newer readers.

food.name: Chicken fingers with honey dill
food.desc: Winnipeg's own condiment - mayonnaise, honey and dill - served with breaded chicken fingers and fries. Locals dip pizza, samosas and burgers in it too.

places.name: Salisbury House
places.note: Manitoba diner chain since 1931; honey dill comes with the chicken fingers as standard.

places.name: The Forks Market
places.note: Riverside food hall where several counters serve chicken fingers with honey dill on the side.

places.name: Dairi-Wip Drive In
places.note: Old-school drive-in that has been doing fries, fingers and soft-serve for decades.

food.name: The Nip
food.desc: Not a slider - Salisbury House's thin, griddled hamburger with fried onions, invented in 1931 and still the city's most nostalgic order, with fries and gravy.

places.name: Salisbury House on Pembina Highway
places.note: Classic booth-and-counter Sals with the full nip, soup and cheese nip line-up.

places.name: Salisbury House on Main Street
places.note: Handy central branch of the 1931 chain; open long hours.

places.name: Salisbury House on Marion Street
places.note: Long-running east-side location, popular for late-night nips.

food.name: Winnipeg rye bread
food.desc: Dense, chewy sourdough rye with a hard crust and caraway seed, baked in North End brick ovens since the 1920s - the base of every local deli sandwich.

places.name: KUB Bakery
places.note: Baking the city's benchmark rye since the 1920s; buy a whole unsliced loaf.

places.name: City Bread
places.note: Another 1930s North End bakery, still turning out rye and kaiser rolls daily.

places.name: Gunn's Bakery
places.note: North End Jewish bakery famous for rye, bagels and cheesecake.

food.name: Perogies and cabbage rolls
food.desc: Potato-and-cheddar dumplings fried in butter with onions and sour cream, plus holubtsi cabbage rolls - Winnipeg's huge Ukrainian community's home cooking.

places.name: The Forks Market
places.note: Ukrainian counters in the market hall do perogy plates all day.

places.name: Ukrainian church perogy suppers
places.note: Parish halls along Main and Selkirk run legendary hand-pinched perogy suppers and sell frozen ones.

places.name: Delis on Selkirk Avenue
places.note: Neighbourhood delis sell perogies, kielbasa and cabbage rolls to take home.

food.name: Fat Boy burger
food.desc: A Winnipeg drive-in invention from the city's Greek diner families: burger loaded with a spiced meat chili sauce, cheese, onion and shredded lettuce.

places.name: VJ's Drive Inn
places.note: Walk-up window institution downtown, cash-only feel and enormous burgers.

places.name: Red Top Drive Inn
places.note: Serving fat boys and shakes since 1959; the classic vinyl-booth version.

places.name: Dairi-Wip Drive In
places.note: Third of the old drive-in trio, with the same chili-sauced burgers.

food.name: Bison and Indigenous prairie cooking
food.desc: Bison steak, burgers and stew alongside Indigenous plates - bannock, three sisters soup, wild rice and Manitoba pickerel from the lakes.

places.name: Feast Cafe Bistro
places.note: Indigenous-owned kitchen known for bannock tacos, bison and Manitoba pickerel.

places.name: Deer + Almond
places.note: Modern small-plates room that cooks prairie ingredients including bison.

places.name: The Forks Market
places.note: Several stalls serve bison burgers and bannock beside the riverwalk.

food.name: Slurpee
food.desc: Winnipeg has been the world's Slurpee capital for more than two decades - frozen convenience-store drinks bought year round, including at minus 30.

places.name: 7-Eleven on Portage Avenue
places.note: Central branch of the chain that made the city the world Slurpee champion.

places.name: 7-Eleven in Osborne Village
places.note: Busy neighbourhood store; the local ritual is mixing three flavours in one cup.

places.name: 7-Eleven on Pembina Highway
places.note: Student-heavy south-end store, one of the highest-volume Slurpee stops.

food.name: Manitoba craft beer
food.desc: A young but strong brewing scene in the old warehouse district - prairie wheat ales, lagers and sours poured in taprooms within walking distance of each other.

places.name: Little Brown Jug
places.note: Taproom in a heritage warehouse; the Belgian-style 1919 is the flagship.

places.name: Nonsuch Brewing Co
places.note: Belgian-inspired brewery with a bright taproom a few blocks away.

places.name: Torque Brewing
places.note: Larger local brewery with a busy tap hall and food trucks outside.

landmarks: The Forks
A historic meeting place at the confluence of the Red and Assiniboine Rivers, now a lively market and riverwalk that anchors the city's identity.
Canadian Museum for Human Rights
An architecturally stunning glass-and-limestone landmark whose glowing Tower of Hope dominates the Winnipeg skyline at night.
Manitoba Legislative Building
A grand Beaux-Arts capitol topped by the gilded 'Golden Boy' statue, widely considered one of Canada's most beautiful legislatures.
St. Boniface Cathedral
The evocative stone facade ruins of a burned 1908 basilica stand as a hauntingly beautiful monument in Winnipeg's French quarter.
Winnipeg Art Gallery – Qaumajuq
Home to the world's largest public collection of contemporary Inuit art, housed in a striking curved white building.
Esplanade Riel
A striking pedestrian bridge over the Red River with a restaurant at its centre, offering one of the city's best photo vantage points.
Exchange District
A National Historic Site of beautifully preserved early-1900s warehouse architecture, cobblestone streets, and murals.
Portage and Main
Canada's famously windy and iconic downtown intersection, long a symbol of Winnipeg itself.
Union Station Winnipeg
A monumental Beaux-Arts railway station designed by the architects of New York's Grand Central Terminal.
Assiniboine Park (Leo Mol Sculpture Garden & English Garden)
A century-old park with formal gardens, bronze sculptures, and a conservatory that is a favorite outdoor retreat and photo spot.

train.note: No international trains - the nearest cross-border rail is Amtrak's Empire Builder well to the south in the United States. VIA Rail's Canadian calls at Winnipeg Union Station two or three times a week between Toronto and Vancouver, and the separate Winnipeg-Churchill train runs north to Hudson Bay in about two days, which is the only land route to Churchill. Book Churchill berths far ahead for the polar bear and beluga seasons.

bus.note: No international coaches. Rider Express (https://riderexpress.ca/) and FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.ca/) run west to Regina, Saskatoon and Calgary and east toward Thunder Bay, with Maple Bus Lines covering some regional routes. Greyhound Canada's closure left the prairies thinly served, so check schedules carefully - some routes run only a few days a week.

ferry.note: Winnipeg is on the prairies with no navigable passenger route, so there are no ferries. River cruises on the Red and Assiniboine operate in summer as sightseeing trips.

half.name: Gimli
half.blurb: Gimli is a lakeside town settled by Icelandic immigrants, with a harbor on Lake Winnipeg and Icelandic heritage sites.

half.name: Lower Fort Garry
half.blurb: Lower Fort Garry is a restored 19th-century Hudson's Bay Company trading post on the banks of the Red River.

half.name: Grand Beach Provincial Park
half.blurb: Grand Beach Provincial Park has wide sand beaches and dunes on the shore of Lake Winnipeg.

half.name: Steinbach (Mennonite Heritage Village)
half.blurb: Steinbach's Mennonite Heritage Village recreates a 1870s prairie settlement with restored buildings and working windmills.
